3.7. Stakeholders 
Since passports are about the governance of the entire product life 
cycle, it may be helpful to understand who the involved actors are, what 
their role is and perspective they hold toward passports. We choose to 
anchor the actor analysis to the most frequently used life cycle variant 
(Stark, 2015, p. 7). This view categorizes the management of a product 
life cycle from the environmental point of view into five phases: (1) raw 
material extraction, (2) manufacturing, (3) transportation, (4) utiliza­
tion (including maintenance), and (5) disposal or recycling. We have 
grouped identified roles based on similar function which resulted in 
twelve actor types that typically interact with a passport (see Fig. 6). 
These roles operate in four distinctive information chains grouped by 
information type: (1) the owners’ chain, (2) the governance chain, (3) 
the financial chain, and (4) the production chain. In the owners’ chain, 
we observe actors that are assigned with the majority of legal re­
sponsibilities for an object, i.e., either by owning it, leasing it or when 
assigned this responsibility from the owner (e.g., facility managers). The 
key objective for these actors is to have access to information that 
support the decision-making regarding the optimal acquiring and 
maintenance of an object according to the needs of the end-user. The 
governance chain is concerned with the task of securing the supply 
system in which the passport is used by verifying the quality, integrity, 
and validity of the information registered in or made accessible by 
passports. In this role of gatekeeper, we typically find the government, 
independent auditors, and passport software providers. The financial 
chain is concerned with financing and insuring an object. The key 
objective is to ensure a correct valuation of an object in order to identify 
the corresponding risk or to determine financing premiums. Finally, the 
production chain is mainly responsible for the physical life cycle oper­
ations performed on the object. This varies from material supply to 
design, production, assembly, distribution, maintenance and disman­
tling activities. The key objective of this group of actors is to document 
their activities in order that others later may benefit from this infor­
mation (including themselves, e.g., in maintenance activities). 
When considering the key opportunities and the key barriers (listed 
unweighted in Table A7, Appendix 5) we observe a misalignment be­
tween the stakes and challenges of different actors; some actors mainly 
benefit while others are charged with data registration and management 
costs. This observation is shared among other studies (e.g., Adisorn et al. 
(2021); Bouwend Nederland (2020); Debacker and Manshoven (2016); 
Greer et al. (2020); Munaro and Tavares (2021)). In some cases, there 
may even be adversarial thoughts against a passport as an information 
gain for one actor may lead to a deterioration of the negotiation position 
of another actor (e.g., recyclers). More generally, the majority of studies 
report that a passport facilitates environmental gains, and often also 
financial gains, hence, observe a societal-cost-benefit business case for 
implementing passports. 
3.8. Goals 
The ’identification of reuse value in the product’ is listed as the 
primary goal of a passport. A major part of this particular goal originates 
from papers related to the BAMB research project (Debacker and 
Manshoven, 2016), but it is used also extensively in direct phrasing or 
similar wording in other projects (Bertino et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2019; 
Merrild et al., 2016; Wittenveen & Bos, 2018).

4.3.3.1.1. Product. Product is central to the use case of this study. 
According to ISO/DIS 59004, product is defined as “physical-based object 
designed for or utilized with a purpose”. Examples of products include 
goods of any type, hardware. and processed materials. This definition is 
adopted to annotate the Product key notion in our ontology. 
In the context of aligning with existing ontologies, we examined 
similar classes from various ontologies: BOT's Element, defined as ‘a 
construction entity with a characteristic technical function, form, or position’; 
BPO's Product, described as ‘a description of any item that can be or is 
offered for sale by vendors or manufacturers’; Brick's Equipment, which 
includes ‘devices that serve all or part of the building and may include electric 
power, lighting, transportation, or service water heating, including, but not 
limited to, furnaces, boilers, air conditioners, heat pumps, chillers, water 
heaters, lamps, luminaires, ballasts, elevators, escalators, or other devices or 
installations’; and REC's Asset, characterized as ‘something which is placed 
inside of a building, but is not an integral part of that building's structure; e.g., 
furniture, equipment, systems, etc.’ Our Product class, adopting a broader 
definition from ISO/DIS 59004, encapsulates these specific entities, 
positioning them as specialized instances within our broader Product 
framework. This enables shared definitions of concepts and promotes 
semantic interoperability and standardization of the key notion. Table 6 
presents the Product module alignment with the existing ontologies in 
the built environment space. 
Following the identified information requirements, products should 
be represented by names and unique identifiers, for which the Name Stub 
and Identifier ontology design patterns are selected; see Fig. 3.
